summary:
Grand Est stands under the national framework of France. Identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage law apply uniformly across the region, and the sources record no regional deviation from the national position on transgender rights.

Custody is the sharpest exposure. Article D248 of the French Criminal Procedure Code requires men and women to be held in separate establishments, so a trans woman whose identity documents record a male sex, which is the case for the vast majority who have not had sex-reassignment surgery, is placed in a men's facility. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 records a detainee hearing other inmates shout "We don't want any women here!" alongside threats of violence.

Adeline Hazan, controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty, states that transgender detainees, overwhelmingly women, are the group that suffers the most in prison. The same feature documents the case of Kara B., an American trans woman held in conditions described as worrying.

The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 following its opinion of 30 June 2010. It finds that serious violations of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees persist in adult prisons, while no such violations were noted in mental-health establishments, closed educational centres or juvenile detention centres. The review covered some forty transgender detainees, with interviews including eight trans women and one trans man, and inspection visits at the Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station.

Placement remains contested in the region's own territory. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October; her incarceration was raised in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the prison system cannot guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of questioning by French border police at an airport, conducted in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits issued a framework decision on trans rights confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the baseline is the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.
tangentialFactors:
The CGLPL's 2021 opinion is a follow-up to its opinion of 30 June 2010, and the mechanism has explained that a new opinion was needed because the earlier one produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology changed in 2016, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees.

Inspection coverage in the 2021 review was concentrated in four prisons and one central police station, all outside Grand Est. Whether the findings on isolation, strip searches and placement apply establishment by establishment within Grand Est is not addressed by the sources.

The A69 motorway case places a trans detainee's conditions before the National Assembly, which is a matter of parliamentary scrutiny rather than a settled guarantee; placement in Tarbes continues while that scrutiny runs.
localsOnly:
French residents held in places of deprivation of liberty are assigned a facility by the sex recorded on identity documents under Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code, with each establishment improvising between special units and isolation that restricts contact with other inmates.

The CGLPL's opinion of 25 May 2021 is binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty and rests on a decade of letters from detained trans people, identifying structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

Residents discriminated against in services can invoke the Défenseur des droits framework decision, which sets out official guidance for service providers, and the anti-discrimination regime that applies nationally.

Legal gender recognition, in force since the 2016 reform, determines subsequent prison placement, so the marker on a resident's documents governs which facility they enter if detained.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records an inspection visit, complaint or enforcement action concerning a place of deprivation of liberty within Grand Est itself; the custodial findings rest on national inspections at establishments elsewhere.

Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has been implemented in Grand Est facilities is unresolved in the sources.

The current placement and conditions of Louna at the time of writing are unresolved; the sources establish her detention since mid-October 2024 and ongoing parliamentary scrutiny, not an outcome.

The Défenseur des droits framework decision is cited for its findings and guidance; its date and the specific services it covers are not given in the inventory.
